Singapore's Ministry of Manpower (MOM) collects reports of workplace injuries from employers under
the Work Injury Compensation Act and of occupational diseases from doctors, and publishes national
statistics each year. This notebook uses fatal, major and minor injuries, occupational diseases and
man-days lost from 2018 to 2025, by industry, with rates per 100,000 workers. Read the module
[README](../README.md) and [data dictionary](../data_dictionary.md) first.

**How to use this notebook**

- Run each code chunk in order (the green arrow in RStudio, or Ctrl/Cmd + Shift + Enter).
- Answer the questions under each **Your answer** heading.
- When you are done, click **Knit** to produce an HTML report to submit.

# Part 0. Load the data

```{r setup, message = FALSE}
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(forcats)

base <- "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/eddiekasner/occupational-safety-health-datasets/main/modules/sg-mom-workplace-safety/data"
read_module <- function(folder, name, ...) {
  local <- file.path("..", "data", folder, name)
  read_csv(if (file.exists(local)) local else file.path(base, folder, name), show_col_types = FALSE,
           ...)
}

# Injuries, occupational diseases and man-days lost by industry (counts and rates)
by_industry <- read_module("tidy", "injuries_by_industry.csv")
# Major and minor injuries by type of injury
injury_types <- read_module("tidy", "injury_types.csv")
# Occupational diseases by type
diseases <- read_module("tidy", "occupational_diseases.csv")

# National figures are the "All industries" rows; industries without a parent are the main ones
national <- by_industry |> filter(industry == "All industries")
main_industries <- by_industry |> filter(is.na(parent), industry != "All industries")
```

Rates are **per 100,000 workers**. From 2021 employers must report every injury with any medical
leave or light duty; MOM publishes minor injuries both ways (`series`). Read the README before
comparing years.

# Part 1. National trends

```{r trend}
national |>
  filter(statistic == "rate") |>
  select(year, measure, series, value) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = year, values_from = value)

national |>
  filter(measure == "Fatal injuries") |>
  select(year, statistic, value) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = statistic, values_from = value) |>
  ggplot(aes(year, count)) +
  geom_col() +
  geom_text(aes(label = rate), vjust = -0.5, size = 3) +
  labs(title = "Workplace fatal injuries (labels: rate per 100,000 workers)", x = NULL,
       y = "Deaths")

national |>
  filter(measure == "Minor injuries", statistic == "count") |>
  ggplot(aes(year, value, colour = series)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point() +
  expand_limits(y = 0) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_comma()) +
  labs(title = "Workplace minor injuries", x = NULL, y = "Injuries", colour = "Reporting rule")
```

**Questions**

1. How did the number and rate of fatal injuries change from 2018 to 2025? Which year stands out?
2. Under the new reporting rule, about twice as many minor injuries are counted as under the old
   one. What kinds of injuries does the old rule leave out? Which series would you use to describe
   the burden of injury, and which to look at trends since 2018?
3. Singapore's fatal injury rate is about 1 per 100,000 workers. Singapore has set a national target
   of below 1.0 by 2028. Why do you think a government chooses the fatal injury rate as its headline
   target, and what are the drawbacks?

**Your answer:**



# Part 2. Industries

```{r industries}
main_industries |>
  filter(measure == "Fatal injuries", statistic == "rate", year >= 2023) |>
  select(year, industry, value) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = year, values_from = value)

main_industries |>
  filter(measure == "Fatal injuries", statistic == "count") |>
  group_by(industry) |>
  summarise(deaths_2018_2025 = sum(value, na.rm = TRUE)) |>
  slice_max(deaths_2018_2025, n = 8) |>
  ggplot(aes(deaths_2018_2025, fct_reorder(industry, deaths_2018_2025))) +
  geom_col() +
  labs(title = "Workplace fatal injuries, 2018 to 2025", x = "Deaths", y = NULL)

main_industries |>
  filter(measure == "Fatal injuries", statistic == "rate",
         industry %in% c("Construction", "Marine", "Transportation & storage", "Manufacturing")) |>
  ggplot(aes(year, value, colour = industry)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point() +
  labs(title = "Fatal injury rate per 100,000 workers", x = NULL, y = NULL, colour = NULL)
```

**Questions**

1. Which industry has the most workplace deaths, and which the highest fatal injury rate? Why can
   they differ?
2. The marine industry (shipbuilding and repair) has a high but very changeable rate. How many
   deaths does it take to change its rate a lot? What does that tell you about rates for small
   industries?
3. MOM reports only selected industries in each table, and the list changes. What problems does
   that create when you compare years?

**Your answer:**



# Part 3. Types of injury

```{r injury-types}
injury_types |>
  filter(severity == "Major", year >= 2022, injury_type != "Total") |>
  group_by(injury_type) |>
  summarise(injuries = sum(value, na.rm = TRUE)) |>
  arrange(desc(injuries))

injury_types |>
  filter(severity == "Minor", series == "New (any medical leave)", year == 2025,
         injury_type != "Total") |>
  mutate(share = round(value / sum(value), 3)) |>
  arrange(desc(value)) |>
  select(injury_type, injuries = value, share)
```

**Questions**

1. What are the most common types of major injury, and of minor injury? Which major injuries
   always count as major, whatever the time off work?
2. Amputations are about a sixth of major injuries. In which kinds of work would you expect them,
   and what controls prevent them?
3. A large share of minor injuries are "Others". Why does a large "Others" group limit what you can
   learn, and how could reporting be improved?

**Your answer:**



# Part 4. Occupational diseases

```{r diseases}
diseases |>
  filter(is.na(group), disease != "Total") |>
  ggplot(aes(year, value, fill = fct_reorder(disease, value, .fun = sum))) +
  geom_col() +
  labs(title = "Confirmed occupational disease cases", x = NULL, y = "Cases", fill = NULL)

diseases |>
  filter(disease %in% c("Total", "Noise-induced hearing loss",
                        "Work-related musculoskeletal disorders", "Occupational skin disease")) |>
  select(year, disease, value) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = disease, values_from = value)

main_industries |>
  filter(measure == "Occupational diseases", statistic == "count", year == 2025) |>
  select(industry, cases = value) |>
  arrange(desc(cases))
```

**Questions**

1. Which two diseases make up most occupational disease cases? Which industry has the most cases?
2. Noise-induced hearing loss cases rose almost fivefold from 2021 to 2023 and then fell. Most cases
   are found by the audiometric examinations that workers exposed to noise must have. Suggest
   reasons for the rise and fall that are about surveillance rather than about noise.
3. Only a few cases of occupational cancer and lung disease are confirmed each year. Why are these
   diseases likely to be under-counted compared with injuries?

**Your answer:**



# Part 5. Man-days lost

MOM estimates the working days lost to workplace injuries with a table of scheduled charges from
the U.S. National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health: each death, or permanent total
incapacity, counts as 6,000 days, and other injuries are scored by the part of the body, the degree
of incapacity and the days of medical leave.

```{r man-days}
main_industries |>
  filter(measure == "Man-days lost", series == "New (any medical leave)", year == 2025) |>
  select(industry, man_days = value) |>
  arrange(desc(man_days)) |>
  mutate(share = round(man_days / sum(man_days, na.rm = TRUE), 3))

national |>
  filter(measure == "Man-days lost", year == 2025) |>
  select(series, value)
```

**Questions**

1. Which industries account for most man-days lost? Is the ranking the same as for deaths?
2. In 2025, the 34 deaths of employees (not counting platform workers) count as 204,000 man-days.
   What share of the total is that? Is counting a fixed number of days for each death a good way to
   combine fatal and non-fatal harm? What else could you use?
